title: Meet the Prophet ﷺ
hook: You say his name in every prayer. Today, meet the man.

screens.text: Every time you say the shahada, you name him: Muhammad ﷺ. Two weeks in, it's time to meet the man himself, not as a name in a sentence but as a person.

events.title: An orphan from Makkah
events.text: Muhammad ﷺ was born in Makkah. He lost his father before birth and his mother at about six. A grandfather, then an uncle, raised him.

events.title: Al-Amin
events.text: Long before any revelation, people called him al-Amin, "the trustworthy," and left their valuables with him [Revealed Path ch. 11].

events.title: The cave of Hira
events.text: He often went alone to a cave called Hira to think and worship. There, the revelation began.

events.title: The Qur'an keeps coming
events.text: The revelation kept coming for twenty-three years.

events.title: Back to Makkah
events.text: The people of Makkah had mocked him and driven him out. When he came back with the upper hand, he took no revenge [Revealed Path ch. 11].

screens.before: Before he was a prophet, people called him al-Amin:

options.feedback: Yes. Even people who later opposed him trusted him with their valuables.
Not quite. He was an orphan, not a king. Al-Amin means the trustworthy.
Not quite. Al-Amin means the trustworthy: people left their valuables with him.

screens.text: **The first word: "Read."** In the cave of Hira, the angel **Jibril** (Gabriel) came to him with the first words of the **Qur'an**: "Recite in the name of your Lord who created" [Q 96:1–5; Bukhari 3].

cards.back: Asked what he did at home, his wife Aisha said he kept busy helping his family, until it was time to pray [Bukhari 676].
A little boy had a pet bird he played with. Whenever the boy was brought to him, the Prophet ﷺ playfully asked him how his bird was doing [Bukhari 6203].
The people of Makkah mocked him and drove him out. When he came back years later with the upper hand, he took no revenge and treated them generously [Revealed Path ch. 11].
The Qur'an says Allah sent him as a mercy to all the worlds [Q 21:107].

screens.text: **A human, not a god.** Muslims don't worship the Prophet ﷺ. He was a man and Allah's last messenger, and only Allah is worshipped.
bubbles: But Muslims love him deeply: the Qur'an calls him an excellent example to follow [Q 33:21] and praises his great character [Q 68:4].
His way of living is called the **sunnah**.

screens.prompt: A friend asks, "So Muhammad is the god of Islam?" What's the accurate answer?

options.text: No. He was Allah's last messenger, a human being. Muslims worship Allah alone
options.feedback: Right. Muslims love and follow him, but worship belongs to Allah alone.
Not quite. Muslims never pray to him. He taught people to worship Allah alone.
Not quite. He was a human being. Jibril was the angel who brought him the revelation.

screens.text: **Why "ﷺ"?** When Muslims say or hear his name, they add *sallallahu 'alayhi wa sallam*. It's a small way of loving him.
bubbles: Muslims also don't draw or picture him, out of respect. You get to know him through what he said and did, and how he treated people.

screens.answer: peace and blessings be upon him
screens.feedback: Muslims add it whenever they say or hear his name. In writing, it's the sign ﷺ.

aiContext:
**Lesson facts**
- Born in Makkah around 570 CE; orphaned young; raised by his grandfather, then his uncle Abu Talib; known as al-Amin before prophethood [Revealed Path ch. 11].
- First revelation in the cave of Hira at about forty, through the angel Jibril: "Recite…" [Q 96:1–5; Bukhari 3]. Revelation continued for 23 years [Revealed Path ch. 10].
- He is a human being and Allah's final messenger, sent as a mercy to the worlds [Q 21:107]; the best example [Q 33:21]; of great character [Q 68:4]. Muslims don't worship him.
- His gentleness: helping at home [Bukhari 676]; asking a little boy about his pet bird [Bukhari 6203; the narration doesn't say the bird died]; generosity to former enemies on returning to Makkah [Revealed Path ch. 11].
- Saying ﷺ after his name; no pictures of him (Spec §11).

**Likely questions**
- *"Why no pictures?"* Out of respect and to keep worship for Allah alone; Muslims across schools avoid depicting him. Keep it short and calm.
- *"Was he married to many women / Aisha's age?"* Common hard question. Give a brief, calm, mainstream answer only if asked, note historical context, and offer to route deeper questions to the imam. Don't argue or dismiss the convert's discomfort.
- *"How is he different from Jesus?"* Both are honored prophets; Muslims believe Jesus is a prophet, not divine. Day 27 covers Jesus in Islam.
- *"Where can I read about his life?"* Suggest asking the mentor for a trusted short biography (sirah). Don't recommend random online channels.
- *"Was he illiterate?"* The tradition holds he couldn't read or write; in the first revelation he said he couldn't read [Bukhari 3].

**Escalate:** detailed questions about his marriages, battles or rulings the convert finds troubling (give a short calm answer, then offer "Ask my imam").

**Don't**
- Don't attribute words to him without a Citation Bank reference; paraphrase hadith, never quote gists as his words.
- Don't describe his physical appearance as if picturing him, and never generate an image.
- Don't use him to pressure ("the Prophet would be disappointed in you").
